Auparavant, Valérie Hébert-Gentile prati: Valérie Hébert-Gentile used to work as a professional cuddler: she gave her clients hugs on request, without batting an eye, until she burned out. “I wanted to make people happier with my hugs, but I didn’t respect my limits,” says Valérie, whom everyone calls Alie.
Dans sa pratique professionnelle de donn: In her work as a professional cuddler, the client was king and their wishes had to be granted, even when a request made Alie uncomfortable. Little by little, a sense of unease set in. It was while taking a training course in the United States that Alie realized she had to say no to requests she didn’t like, even with a client.
« Ça va de toute façon se ressentir sur: “It’s going to show in the hug anyway if I’m not comfortable,” she explains. She now practises cuddle therapy with Calia, Montréal’s first cuddle therapy institute, but with consent at the heart of her workshops. She is convinced that hugs are a valuable tool for teaching consent.
Durant ses ateliers, les participants so: During her workshops, participants are simply invited to hug each other to practise the concept in a safe and caring environment. The goal is for them to apply it in their daily lives and in their relationships.
Mme Hébert-Gentile a imaginé un acronyme: Ms. Hébert-Gentile came up with an acronym to make the fundamental notions of consent easier to remember: RÉELS, for Réversible, Éclairé, Enthousiaste, Libre and Spécifique (reversible, informed, enthusiastic, free and specific). Saying yes once doesn’t necessarily commit you to everything. “In my generation, we weren’t taught that! If I say yes once, I’m supposed to go all the way! But I can take it back, I have the right!” she exclaims. Agreeing to one particular thing doesn’t mean consenting to everything: consent is always reversible and specific to a particular action.
Une notion sur laquelle elle insiste bea: It’s a notion she insists on a great deal. Consent must also be free of any coercion, any power dynamic and any fear of hurting the other person. It is both informed, because everyone must be aware of themselves and their intentions, and enthusiastic.
« Il faut se poser la question et se dir: “You have to ask yourself the question and tell yourself that if you’re hesitating, it’s because one part of you doesn’t want to and another part is trying to convince itself. When in doubt, don’t!” sums up Ms. Hébert-Gentile.
À ceux qui critiquent la complexité de l: To those who criticize how complicated the notion of consent is, and the idea of asking permission every time to make sure the other person is enthusiastic, she answers that “asking isn’t necessarily boring.”
En couple, demander peut être sexy. Entr: In a couple, asking can be sexy. Among friends or family, asking questions can prompt reflection the other person wouldn’t have had if you hadn’t asked for their opinion. And if asking isn’t possible or a mistake happens, there’s always the option of talking about it: “It’s important to stay alert and be aware of the other person’s reactions and needs,” she says.
<strong>La roue du consentement pour com: The wheel of consent as a way to understand
Les exercices que Mme Hébert-Gentile pro: The exercises Ms. Hébert-Gentile offers in her workshops are similar to the wheel of consent, a tool inspired by the BDSM community, where consent is central and codified. The wheel was devised by Betty Martin, a life coach and trainer. Other educators and practitioners use it to teach consent, including Anne-Flore Baron, Love & Life, somato-psychopedagogue, and Emmanuelle Duchesne, founder of the Slow Sex Love Life collective.
Elles donnent entre autres des ateliers: Among other things, they lead personal development workshops devoted to positive sexuality. While sexuality is a central theme of these workshops, it isn’t ever-present: the exercises they offer touch on every aspect of life. The wheel of consent is a game that can be played every day to create moments of practice and exploration, whether with your child, your partner, a parent or a friend.
La roue permet d’explorer deux types de: The wheel lets people explore two types of postures: giving and receiving. “The top two quadrants are about the action of touching, and the bottom two involve being touched,” explains Anne-Flore Baron. Players take turns exploring the actions in these quadrants. On top of that comes the notion of a gift. On the left, you offer or grant something to the other person for their pleasure. On the right, the gift is received.
« Cette notion de cadeau permet une nuan: “This notion of a gift allows for an essential nuance: the person who touches can do so to meet their own desire or to satisfy the other person’s,” adds Ms. Baron. The wheel makes it possible to practise every aspect of consent, since everyone generally has one role they’re comfortable in and another they’re uneasy in. For example, stubborn gender and personality stereotypes make some people more inclined to act or take, based on their own needs. Conversely, others are generally in the position of service, of care for the other, to the point of forgetting their own needs. While these patterns are already changing, the wheel of consent is an additional aid for breaking free of them.
Cet outil est un moyen de bousculer les: This tool is a way to shake up norms, reverse roles and take ownership of oneself again. And to do so with transparency and honesty.
« Si l’un a envie de toucher les fesses: “If one person wants to touch the other’s buttocks for their own pleasure, they have to say so without disguising the request as a favour: ‘A little massage would do you good, no?’” Ms. Baron says, illustrating with a joke.
Pour Emmanuelle Duchesne, auteure de <em: For Emmanuelle Duchesne, author of 50 exercices de slow love et sex meditation, it’s important to become aware of all of one’s characteristics (social class, origin, religion, etc.) and to free oneself from them so they no longer stand in the way of consent. There are always situations where it’s harder to say no. So you have to understand why and free yourself from those constraints. She explains that participants in her workshops have been able to apply the lessons she teaches directly in their daily lives.
« Une personne qui est venue dans mes at: “One person who came to my workshops told me that once, on the bus, a passenger was pressed up against her even though there was plenty of room. Instead of putting up with the discomfort, she asked him to give her some space. It went very well, and she didn’t get worked up,” says Ms. Duchesne happily. For her, practising consent is a way to regain the ability to act, without feeling like a victim and without creating tension.
<strong>Comment répandre un consentement: How can we spread free, enthusiastic and informed consent?
Pourtant fort intéressants, ces ateliers: Although they are very interesting, these workshops are still far from widespread. They generally attract people who are already familiar with the subject, mostly women. For Emmanuelle Duchesne, comprehensive consent education is needed. “We aren’t trained in consent. At some point in our lives, we realize that it’s now up to us to choose, not our parents. Giving your opinion exposes you to humiliation and makes you vulnerable. But it shouldn’t be like that,” she explains. The fight against rape culture involves teaching consent in schools, but also to older people. Valérie Roy, a professor at Université Laval and a member of the research group Masculinités et société, believes attitudes can change through prevention.
« Comment changer les mentalités ? Il fa: “How do you change attitudes? You have to reach the whole population, all age groups,” she says. For example, drunk-driving prevention campaigns have changed behaviours and attitudes over the long term. Ms. Roy believes that what matters is how we talk about consent. “If we talk about it negatively, it gives the idea of deprivation. Conversely, a positive approach can help people move past preconceived ideas and clichés, and lead each person to ask themselves what kind of practice they like,” she says. This can mean bringing the person back to what they have lived through, to make them aware of the consequences and develop empathy.
« Il faut incarner le consentement afin: “We have to embody consent so that everyone can make it their own,” she says. “Embody consent” to offer a model everyone can identify with, regardless of gender. “Embody consent” to move past gender stereotypes, which men also endure and perpetuate. And finally, “embody consent” to live relationships on an equal footing with others.
Deux jeux pour s’exercer au consentement: Two games for practising consent: The yes-and-no game, to understand that saying “yes” or “no” belongs to the person who speaks the words. A asks B if they can put a hand on B’s shoulder. B says yes. Later in the game, as A puts a hand on B’s shoulder again, B says no. It’s a way of showing that consent depends on the moment, the mood, the desire, in short on each person’s mental and physical state. This exercise may seem formal at first glance, but it often prompts laughter and deep discussions.
Le jeu du désir, pour pratiquer le conse: The desire game, for practising consent without touching. One woman asks her friend what her desire is. The friend has to say whatever comes to mind, even if it’s far-fetched and unrealistic. The one who asked the question must pay attention to what the expressed desire does to her (tingling, laughter, anger, shutting down), say so, then ask another question. The two friends then switch roles. “For me, this game shows that just because a desire is expressed doesn’t mean it has to be fulfilled. It teaches you to enjoy the sparkle of life in desire without getting carried away. You savour the desire,” says Anne-Flore Baron.
